plan.hypothesis: H₀: μ ≤ 0 vs. H₁: μ > 0 (one-sided test)
assumptions: One-sample design with fixed mean under null hypothesis (μ₀ = 0)
Common standard deviation σ = 0.5 applies to the population
Test statistic follows t-distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom under null
scientific_notes: One-sided test has greater sensitivity to the specified direction of effect than a two-sided test

answer.summary: For a one-sample t-test comparing a normally distributed outcome against a null mean, testing for a true mean increase of 0.2 units with population SD 0.5 using a one-sided test at α=0.05, the minimum integer sample size to achieve 80% power is 41 participants. This design achieves 80.86% power, exceeding the target. The preceding design (n=40) yields 79.97% power, confirming that n=41 is the smallest admissible sample size.
answer.method: one_sample_t: Two-stage analytic inversion using pwr::pwr.t.test(). The continuous solution n=40.03 is rounded up to the next integer. Power verified at both n=41 and n=40 to confirm the boundary.
assumptions: Outcome is normally distributed with known population SD σ = 0.5
One-sample design testing H₀: μ ≤ 0 vs. H₁: μ > 0 (one-sided, alternative='greater')
True population mean under the alternative is μ = 0.2 units
Test statistic follows non-central t-distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom under the alternative
limitations: Power analysis assumes population parameters are known (mean difference and SD); actual power depends on accurate specification of these effect parameters
No interim analysis or sequential testing considered
Assumes normality is reasonable for the outcome; non-normal data may require different test or larger sample
Does not account for potential losses to follow-up or dropout (if applicable to study duration)
Rounding convention uses ceiling function; alternative rounding strategies may yield different integers

executions.code:
# Install and load pwr package for power analysis
if (!requireNamespace("pwr", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("pwr")
}
library(pwr)

# Define parameters
effect_size <- 0.2 / 0.5  # Cohen's d = mean_difference / SD
alpha <- 0.05
target_power <- 0.80
alternative <- "greater"  # one-sided test

# Use pwr.t.test for one-sample t-test
# Type "one.sample" requires effect size as Cohen's d
result <- pwr.t.test(
  n = NULL,  # Solve for n
  d = effect_size,
  sig.level = alpha,
  power = target_power,
  type = "one.sample",
  alternative = alternative
)

# Extract the sample size (continuous solution)
continuous_n <- result$n
print(paste("Continuous sample size:", continuous_n))

# Round up to next integer (smallest integer achieving target power)
min_n_integer <- ceiling(continuous_n)
print(paste("Minimum integer sample size:", min_n_integer))

# Verify achieved power at this integer sample size
verification <- pwr.t.test(
  n = min_n_integer,
  d = effect_size,
  sig.level = alpha,
  type = "one.sample",
  alternative = alternative
)
achieved_power <- verification$power
print(paste("Achieved power at n =", min_n_integer, ":", round(achieved_power, 6)))

# Also check power at n-1 to confirm this is the minimum
if (min_n_integer > 1) {
  previous <- pwr.t.test(
    n = min_n_integer - 1,
    d = effect_size,
    sig.level = alpha,
    type = "one.sample",
    alternative = alternative
  )
  power_previous <- previous$power
  print(paste("Power at n =", min_n_integer - 1, ":", round(power_previous, 6)))
}

# Output results in required format
results_df <- data.frame(
  metric = c("sample_size", "achieved_power", "effect_size_cohens_d", "alpha", "target_power"),
  value = c(min_n_integer, achieved_power, effect_size, alpha, target_power),
  unit = c("participants_total", "probability", "unitless", "probability", "probability")
)

print("\nSummary:")
print(results_df)

# Emit result in required format
cat("POWER_AGENT_RESULT=")
cat(jsonlite::toJSON(
  list(results = results_df),
  auto_unbox = TRUE,
  digits = 15
))
